for these atrocities it is a question for each constituency and for every elector; and it especially concerns electors in this part of the country, who by Silks of omission or commiasion have had so much to do with providing Lord SALISBURY with a mechanical majority. Many constituencies have, it is true, been basely betrayed for, despite warning upon wonting that there was no alternative be- tween Conciliation and Coercion, it was hardly possible to believe that candidates who talked about "equal laws" would, when they got within the walls of St. Stephen's, vote for the enactment and enforcement of the newt unequal laws that the United Kingdom has ever km ovn. It was the one great cry of Lord HARTINIITON, when Mr. tsrscross introduced his Home Rule Bill, that the Parliament of had no mandate to grant Home Rule to Ireland ; hut will his lordship dare to say, or will any Unionist dare to say, that the present Parliament had a mandate from the nation to apply Coercion to Ireland'," The mandate was all the other way—the pledges were all in the direction of Conciliation to Ireland ; it was tn. be a message of peace by granting self- government, if not Home Rule. But instead of ndf-government, the liberties of the people are strangled by a villainons Coercion Act, while the symbols of the message of peace are a baton and battering-ram. As Mr. GiAnsrosr, said at Tor- quay. on Monday. there never wits" a ease where a majority constitating a 1101180 of Commons and guiding its proceedings has no grossly trampled upon the engagements by which it obtained the suffrages of the people." What, it may be asked, is the remedy for this shameful violation of pledges There was a time when a man had to lose his head for turning traitor ; but in these I days it is mat, sufficient that the traitor, if he is . a member of Parliament, should lose his seat. And the electors who feel that they have been misrepresented, who are conscious of having been betrayed, owe it to themselves to see that this is done at the next election. They may have had their doubts as to the right course three years ago, but to-day the path of duty lies plainly before I them ; let them follow it, and aid in the triumph of a righteous cause.

Toe controversy as to the merits Vaccination and demerits of vaccination seems Cofffr",,,,Y. to have been greatly stimulated by • Dr. CaRIiIIITON'S article on vaccination, in the new issue of the " EncycloPaxlia Britannic." The opponents of vaccination—of compulsory vaccin- ation in particular—are, naturally enough, making the advantage they have gained through having the efficacy of the "Jesmerian rite," as they mono- times call it, questioned in the great Encyclopaedia, while ti the other hand, the heavy professional batallions who support vaccination, are not to be assailed with impunity. Dr. CREIGHTON holds thatl the d gers of vaccination have been very much uuder-rated, and the benefits to be derived from it largely exaggerated. Among the diseases which vaccination may bring upon a patient, he enumerates vaccine' syphilis. skin eruption, jaun- dice, vaccine ulcers and erysipelas. He regards maudlin. —to escape which vathination has been made compulsory—as a" foreign pestilence," which is mainly influenced by sanitary conditions, and ! which would, in time, probably disappear of itself if vaccination were abandoned. This latter argu- ment is muloulitedly one of the weightiest that opponents 14 vathination are accustomed to put forward. It will probably be denied by ambody that improvements in sanitary conditions halve been the means of repressing other diseatha than smallpox, which in former centuries were veritable scourges of mankind. According to Dr. B. W. RICHARDSON, no malady, mice originated, has ever actually died out." The Black Death. we are told, lingers in malignant typhus, and the great plague of Constantinople, the plague of the fifth century, has even in our time been net with in England, in France, and in America. li, then, in spite of the fact that we always have the germs of these and other dire diseaaes amongst us, their ravages are limited to the smalleat dimensions it is an obvious inference that this is due mainly, if not entirely, to the improvementa in sanitation and increase of medical skill, which distinguish this age from the ages that have gone before it. And , this being is,, it must at Once be admitted that anti-vaccinators have at least the ground of analogy on which to lame their argument, that ! atuall-pox might adna, be kept in check by the 1 same agencies, without the special and particular! device of vaccination. If, in addition, they ran! show that vaccination carries with it dangers ! which are as gre:it or greater than those it is intended to avert, their case, of course, becomes , at .nice irresistible. But in theirattempt to dothis! the Mils against them are extremely heavy. In the first place, the medical profession in all but united in its support of vaccination, and this is a question in which medical men are, above all others, qualified to judge. In the second place, statistim of apparently irrepreachable authenticity are remarkably significant in regard to the good effects of vaccination. Some of these are quoted by Mr. H. PRISSTON-FHOWAS who assails Dr. CREIGH- TON'AiiIuiIIiOIIII in this mouth's "National Review." A vaccination census taken by the Poor-law Guardians of St. Pancras, in 113(1 1, wont to show that of 71,213 persons over 10 years of age, who had undergone a single vaccination, 2,013, or 2:ff per cent., were found to be marked with smallpox ; of the 39,83:i who had Imesa re. vaccinated only 20 or o.os per cont. were so marked: and of the 1,377 unvaccinated no loss than 8:17, mr 62'2 per cent., Imre unmistakable traces of the disease. Acthrding to these figures.the chances .4 an unvaccinated person getting smallpox, an coin- : pared with the chances of a persma who has been • re-vaccinated, ere MS 777 to one. Mr. PERsTON- , THOMAS &din, ponds dnit that at the London Snmll-1 pox Hospital it ha., been customary for fifty years. to re-vaccinate the nurses and servants engaged ! there, and, with one exception, there neverdur- ing the fifty years been a ease if smallpox amongst them. The exception was that of a gardemm, who refused to be re-vaceinabel ink the ground , that his duties did not take him into the hospital. Statistics such as these, if their accuracy tamed be impugned, are bound tlm carry weight. and in the minds ,4 many people are suffiiient to justify , vaccination, compulsory or otherwise. The vaecina- tion controversy undoubtedly involves matter; of the greatest public iniporraTlCO, and it in Wane (Ruse for satisfaction that an Royal Commission, with Lord lIRRSITIELL alt Chairman, haw been appointed to deal With it iii lb, latest phases.

in the peculiar nature of the circum- stances. An accident to an excursion train is always more than ordinarily distressing : contrast- ing, as it does, in its saddening results, with the gay spirit in whii:h the pleasure-seekers have eon:- mowed the kinrnry In this case the contrast is heighten...l and the distress intensified by: the fact that the bulk of the eseursionista were ehildreta who hare been &emit...toned like lambs whilst at •

innocent play. The death-roll exceeds seventy, and, as there are some now lying at the Infirmary in a critical condition, it is to be feared that it will be still further augmented. Naturally everybody : is asking—What was the cause of the disaster % There is some uncertainty as yet as to the facts; I, but so far as they Mil be ascertained it would scion that the mtg. haul snore than it could do to take the train up the hill beyond Armagh ; that the officials divided the train with a view to getting it over the hill in two sections ; and that the portion of the tram left without engine, and insufficiently cogged, ran down the incline, with ever-increasing speed, until it crashed into an ordinary train from Armagh. On the face of it, there would appear to have neen negligence, or a grave error of judgment, and four officials have been placed under arrest. If the engine was not equal to the work it had to do, the proper thing would have been to return with the train for a second engine. it was thought- lemmas bordering on madness to attempt to leave a number of railway carriages on a steep incline, ' with the risk, if a cog slipped, of their rushing to destruction. Putting the break on ander such . circumstances was useless ;it is what the guard did ' when he found his section of the train moving; but as he says, " you might as well have tried to stop , her with a hit of straw.- It may be that the break was not and eould not be applied in time : but this and other letermined points will probably be settled in the inquiry which is to be held by MAJOR GENERAL HVIVIIINNON on behalf of the Board of Trade. Meantime, Armagh is a place of sorrow and of anguish, for there is ninny a RACHEL mounting for her children because they are not.

The schoolboy who wrote of the famous fabled , strewn as" the River Stynx " may be said to have " improved the occasion, for he showed regard alike to sense and sound. Can it be that he had lived for a summer on the river Mersey, or does he hail from the neighbourhood of Sankey Brook

There has been weather and weather during Whitsuntide. Whilst it was wet and disagreeable, on Whit-Monday, in the South and in the Mid- lands, it was beautifully fine in the North. It is a tradition that there is good weather at Whit- suntide in the lake district ;it is therefore the right place to go" laking."

• I When the hop-growers of Kent arose, on Mon- ' day morning, they found that their gardens had been swept with the beSOM of destruction. Crops of all kinds were terribly damaged, nod fruit trees had not only young 'fruit, but young limbs lopped oft Under such circumstances it was impossible of course to sing Hail smiling

Sir Gilbert Greenall has not vet addressed his constituents. In times past he had nothing to say it is true—but he used to say it. Why, oh why, jobs 'dark and silent as the moon? He might at least explain how it happens that he has not yet voted in favour of " autonomy for Ireland as promised in his election address for I oSS.

IDaniel Crosby, a labourer living in Scotland- cowl, was brought before the Warrington magis- trates, on Monday, and fined 10s, and costs for being drunk and disorderly. As this was Daniel's sixty-second am caroller, it is evident that he labours in the wrong direction. " A Daniel come to judgment " is well enough once in a way, but sixty-two times l—that is too touch of a good thing. At the same court, the magistrates had before ' them a German named Bombina, a player on a concertina, who had kicked up a "shindy," and • broken a "windy," at Red Lion Inn. He was , lectured, fined .I.s. and costs, and ordered to mike ! good the damage to the window—and little enough when a German band (of one) has introduced no ' much diikord.

On Tuesday afternoon the Shah witnessed "an historical procession, organised by the brewers of Berlin, and illustrating the development of beer, the consumers thereof being more prominently displayed than the producers.' But the show was incomplete: there does not seem to have been ' any representation of either a gaol, a workhouse, or a lunatic asylum.

The " Star " says: —For once the great Pears lies heon beaten in the advertising lino. Everyone ; knows the famous advertisement. " Good morn- ; ing have you used Pear's soap " The °thee day one of the big dailies bad. the following, immediately opposite the Pear's advertisement, "Yes, hut Cleaver's is better. Good evening." Cleaver had rather tho "laugh "on Pears there. .

The disaster in Pensylvania has led to some die- , mission as to the safety or otherwise of the new I dam at Vyriiwy. One authority describes it as , "0 solid stone dam,- while another insists that "it i is cot a masonry dam thrmighout as it should he.- [ The discussion may rouse a little alarm, but it can Ido no serious harm ; indeed, it will be of special !service if it results in the strengthening of a weak spot—should a weak spot be found.

There have been so many thunderstorms in Paris since the Eiffel tower was completed that there are Parisians who believe the tower is the cause of them. What is to be done It will never Ii to take it down, or blow it op, until the Exhibi- tion is over. Is there nobody equal to inventing a Thunderstorm Protection Pill There ought to be descendants somewhere of the genius Who once made pills for protection against earthquakes.

The Tory papers usually strike at random when Mr. Diadsione is concerned. The " Glois• says that the Liberal leader "dooms it expedient to reserve his bests flights of imagination for ha:Adios where political knowledge is at a low ebb." Con- sidering that Devonshire sends seven Coercionist representatives iind Only one Home Ruler to Parliament, the " Globe," without intending it, has given the Unionists a slap in the face.

A New York telegram says The American Executing Company has just been inisirporated at Chicago with a capital of 4:25,000. It is started to take over from the sheriffs HY a going concern the execution of criminals throughout the States, spathe promoters say that those taking up shares ' may reasonably expect a good dividend." What are we to make of this Is it a grim juke, or a grim speculation In either case it is ghaatly, ghoulish.

At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, a tradesman named Isaac MOO wag Sllllllllollod for keeping gunpowder on unregistered premises. Whim asked if he was guilty, he answered :—" An to being guilty or mat, I would rather not sty either.' He was like the Irishman who when a similar ilintsti.ala was put said:—" Sure, yer banner, an how eau I tell till I hear the nridence " lenience" was forthcoming in Mite's case, and he was lined 3s. and costs.

The country owe, melt to the providence of trade and friendly adies —more than can ever be really known. As. Durant if I licioventer, wife of a deceased railway gnard, has :plat written It warm letter of thanks :wknowledging the receipt of over MVO from the Orphan Fund of the Amid-

gamated Society of Railway Servants. She :Ode— "by the time my youngest child attains hie thirteenth birthday, I shall have leceived in all nearly 1:2110." This is better than having to fall , back upon the rates ; sind it is evidence, too, of the admirable way in which this particular society is fulfilling its mission.

The deference paid to Mrs. Maybrick as a pri- soner is the talk of town and country. She is allowed to shroud her features in court, as if so much virtue were not to be lightly looked at and she is provided with a particularly easy chair, lest 1 her tender form should suffer a moment's discom- fort. Would it have been the same if she had not been a' lady r A lady forsooth ! Taking a liberty with Sluarespeare, may we not say ? Mate sin with gold. And tire strong arm of justice finds a lounge ; Clothe it in rags, there's net a stool to sit on.

The life and labours of Father 11111liell are to be worthily commemorated: and the Prince of WOCI, with characteristic breadth, has placed himself at thehead of the movement. It is pleasant to see such men workino together in such a cause 119 the Archbishop of Canterbury, Cardinal Manning, Principal Fairbairn, the Rev. C. H. Spurgeon, the Bishop of Londim, and Dr. Vaughan, Bishop of Salford, Mr. Gladstone, Mr. John Morley, Lord flartington and Lord Randolph Churchill. They recognise that there is something better than squabbling over creeds. • . _ .
For males of faith let graceless zealots fight His can't be wrong whose life Is it. the right.

Doing the past week Mr. Barnett Pareeze;:Tfie, author of •` From the Twilight .d Judaism to the Brightmws of Christianity," has occupied the Public Hall a Runconi, with his Prussian Choir and his diorainns ; and the success that has attended the entertainments has em- boldened Mr. Panszer to prolong his stay for another wok. As there is a change of programme etch evening the diorama can he visited on More than one occasion with pleasure and profit. The views are works of art, and an, displayed by means of an apparatus specially constructed for Mr. Pareszer, and Mr. .1.1%. Cummings,its manipuiator.has had 20 years expen bine° in this kind of work. Mr. Panszar is a model guide and his bright and entertaining descriptions were listened to with rapt attention. The choir is a body of vocalists ant instrumentalists that exhibit careful training and marked ability in every department. On Monday evening the subject of the diorama was" Round the World," Tuesday, "Canada," Wednesday, " Europe," Thursday, "-Paris," and last night •• Wales." The excellency and refinement `if the entertainment is tostifiol to by the fact tile each evening a local clergy- man has occupied the chair ; the vicar (Rev. A. Mait- land Wood) the Res. Dr. Preston, the Rev. Dr. Gasteldi, and the Rev. J. D. Thomas have officiated. ST. JACOB'S OM.

div.head: Snit.. B. WALKERS RETURN.
div.p: Snit.. B. WALKERS RETURN.

Sir A. B. Walker, Bart., has once more returned to his Lancashire home, Gatemen. Grange, but it is to be regretted that his search for health in the genial climate of Southern Europe has not been entirely successful. It will be remembered that, after the revere illness which made hie friends so anxious his medical adviser counselled a sojourn in the south of France, and there he was joined by Gr. Henry Gorst, of Iluyton. During Sir •ndrew's stay on the Continent. his health has varied, but it was hoped that he would be thoroughly restored by the time he returned to the neighbourhood. It is thought that when he has rested after his travels lie will be better.

The Church of St. Michael, If uyton, was on Wednesday filled by a fashionable throng to witness the marriage of Lieutenant Joseph Honner, R.N., H.M.S. Alexandra, Mediterranean Squadron, son of Mr. Joseph flonner,Clerk to the Crown, county Tip- perary, and Miss Francesca de Sanpayo Reid Shand, Elub.villa, !Layton, daughter of the late William Walter Shand, of Antigua, West Indies, niece of the late Sir Alerander Reid. and COl.lll to the newly- appointed Judge Shand. The best man was Lieutenant H. F. Mackay, Royal Marine Artillery. The bride, who wore a white broeaded silk train, draped with crffiet clone and Imo with coronet of orange blossom, and veil fastene;l with diamond ornaments, and carrying a bouquet of rare exotics, was given away by her brother Mr. James Sinclair Shand. The wedding party included between forty and fifty invited guests. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. Cattail Venrhyn. Oaring the after- noon Mrs. Shand held a reception. A tire, fortunately not very serious in its results, broke out at the works of the Atlas Chemical Com- pany about two o'clock on Sunday morning. In these works, salt cake is manufactured by Messrs. Hargreaves and litibinsion's patent, in which a iind of blow pipe plays a prominent VIA. The process requires to be carefully watched,. and the blow pipe shut off at the proem. time, otherwise a stream of not air arising fnon fine of the burners, escapes film the cylinder, and considerable danger is the consequent, On Saturday night two men were left in eharge,but at theliour statol, the hot air escaped, and impinging on the woodwork lathe vicinity quickly set it in flaines. The men on duty @sedan inch pipe, but the sinall quantity of water :bey were thus enabled to throw upon the fire had not WWII !lee, and the flatoes spread to the roof and flooring. An alartn was Aèn and ia WI minutes after 1 they were WM171441, the Fire Brigade were on ilie vane under tit: foonnand of Deputy Suptrinterident Dux. leiry. div.p: ELFICI9RAL ARRAS IN NORTHWICR DIVISION.

' The sub-committee appointed by the Cheshire • County Council to re-artange the electoral areas of the Morthwich Parliamentary 11•' on met at . North wich Courthouse on Wednesday. Colonel France Hayhurst, C.C., J.P.,presided.and there were • present alderman C. Kay, Councillor E. H. • Moss, and Councillor Speakman. Mr. W. Hand- ley Liberal 5g.-at, and Mr. C. J. Hughes Conservative agent, were present. The duties of the Committee were (I), to consider and re-arrange, if niyessary. the Parlia- mentary polling districts ; 12) to consider and re-arrange the polling places for Parliamentary elections and also (3) the place, at which the revising barrister shall hold courts for revising the list of eler!ors ; Olt to consider and fix the polling districts and eltytoral IliviAions for county council eleetions ; I'sl to eon- she and fix the polling pl:we for county council . election,. The committee went the nigh a wrim of pro- posals drawn op by Mr. Handl, y. and agreed to by Mr. Hughes, and they aveni :tempted in their entirety. With p regard to County Council divisions, it was pointed out that at prenint the areas so overlapped the Parliamen- tary divisions that it was desirable sumo ihang' should be made, and as this could only be done Inv conferring with the committee as a whole, it was decided to submit the scheme suggested by Mr. Handley to the General • Committee of the County Council. In his draft, Mr. Handley stated that as at present arrangod satisfactory reViSiOn of the County Council divisions seemed impossible and it was desirable to bring these areas within the boundaries of the Parliamentary 11141- MM., Mr. Handley shovreal how thri could ho ilone by dividing the Northwich Parliamentary Division 5,1,11 electoral areas for County Council purpmis ; each division having an average of 8,215 voters. The num- her of members would than be reduced from ten to seven three nienthers being given to 82 townships in other five parliamentary divisii ins) with apopulation of 19,088, which were at present included in Norttiwi ii, Parlia- tnentary, Division.

That another Whitsuntide has coins and gone, and the people are now settling down to their daily routine of labour. While Widnesians made no show nt home, and hurried away from the sight of the dusty roads and dull brick buildings of the chemical metropolis, the Runeornians remained in their ancient town to witness the annual demon- etrations of clubs and Sunday school scholars. The weather being dull, the processions did not present se bright an appearance as on many previous occa- sions, but the displays were nevertheless a success. That one wonders why the schools cannot unite to have one grand procession, like the members of the clubs, which are composed of persons of all denominations. Several times, on Monday, confitsion occurred through schools passing each other in opposite dinwtions and besides spoiling the effectiveness of the demonstration, causol great inconveniente. Perhaps the queMion of precedence is the stumbling block, but to an un- prejudieol observer, it does seem old that people who are striving to attain the same heaven, canon slow a little 1101.1. of that love towards each other which is said to be the special attribute of the celestials. That differences of creed did not prevent the Catholics and Dissenters from going togetheeand it was a thousand pit i. the churches did not unite with tile chapels to form one happy family. That the excursion to the residence of the Grand Old Man. on Tuesday, was an unqualified SLIM,s from every point of view, the only cause for regret being that Mr. Gladstone was for away in the West. The castle, the park, the villa. he and t church were all the cents."( ! great interest'', and it was not unpleasing, to see that ! several Conservatives had made the pilgrimage to the shriseof the greatest Englishman of Ins time. . . . a. .

Hamm Bressums IN COLLISION.—A Lloyd's Suez telegram says the British steamers tilen-Roy and Akaba have been in collision. Both were damaged, but will prnceed after being surveyed. INDIANS ON THE IVARPAiH.—According to intelligence received in New York from Minni,ota, a party of Chip- pewa Indians ham- made a raid upon the sewers in the vicinity of Mille Lacks Lake, killing several Swedes.
YELLOW FEVER AT SOU:IIIAMPTON.

Last night's '• Gazette " publishes a Privy Council notice entering the royal mail steamer Neva, Mild) has arrived at Southampton with yellow fever aboard, to be placed in quarantine together with her passengers and crew until further orders. Tax PONSONBY ESTATE EVICHONS.

A meeting was held e Youghal on Thursday evening, ,at which several English visitors spoke, to protest against evictions being carried out on the Ponsenby estate. A crowd with bands afterwards serenaded wane tenants imprisoned in gaol, but the polieedispersed I them, using their batons freely. _ THE CIIETWEND-DURHAM ARBITRATION.

The Clietwynd-Durham arbitration was resumed at the Law Courts on Friday.—Sherrard, the trainer, was further cross-examined. lie denied that Wood was the real owner of the hors. which ran in his iSherrard'si name He was unable to produce documents showing ihe imbue of the transactions when Wood bought horses for him. The crosssexamination was postponed, Sir Charles Russell demanding the production of the dominants.
MURDER IN. EAST CEMBERLAND.

! Ors Thursday Mr. CarWirc2eni.inser.-for East Comb, land, cvmpleted the inquest upon Sabra Troughear. ' houselimper, whose dead body was found lying on the roadside about three mites west of Carlisle fa.ct Sunday week. The coroner said he could not suggest hose the , jury could entertain any doubt that Kerr committed the ' attack on the deceased, and was therefore responsible for her death. The jury returned a verdict of Wilful ! murder " against trillium Kerr.

MIL GLADSTONE IN THE WEST. Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, Mr. H. Gladstone, Mr. Arnold Morley, Mr. Cyril Flower, and others, left Tintagel shortly after ten on Friday morning and drove to Launceston to fulfil the last of his series of Cornish engagements. At several places en route there was great cheering, and there was a demonstration at Launceston, which was moiled at 1245. At the station gate he was welcomed by tlie members of the Liberal Club and association.

In the afternoon Mr. illaktone addrewsl a great meeting held in the open air on Castle Green. In i ponse to an address from the Liberals of the Parliamen- I Lary division, he said he accepted with the greatest I pleasure the addrem which had been pnisented to him. The only criticism he had to make was that no terms were too favoutuble to himself. Since he came to Cornwall he began to think that the whole population a. Liberal.

The death of Huston makes, with the carman who died from excitement and the child Steensen found in the kF,ei urn Thursday night, a total list of 76 fatalities. On Friday morning there were half a down funerals, and for hours services for the dead were going on in the churches. The town isdinolated and people do nothing but talk about the eataatrophe. In reply to a telegram received fb am Balmoral on Thursday conveying the synipatlietic tptineo of the Queen. Mr. M'Latnan, chairman of the town commis- sioners. telegraphed to the Prince of Wales as follows I Loyal respects and humble thanks for kind sympathy, I will convey contents of telegram to bereaved

relation." Later on a telegram FM received from Sir Fleetwood Edwards. intimating that the messages on- veying the Queen's sympathy had been sent by hint by her Majesty's coimnand. In acknowledging this • am- munication Mr. M'Larti. telegraplesl :--"lirateful for kind sympathy of our beloved Queen." Business is still practically suspended. and the only sounds that disturb the dull monotony of the stmt. are those ocvasiimed by the funeral processions which follow each other at frequent intervals to the church- yard outside the city.

At the Newton Petty Seseions on Saturday, a touching reference was made to the death of the late Mr. Joseph Evans JP., D.L. The tnagistrates on the Bench were Captain T. E. Withington, and I Mestint. T. J. Gillespie, W. F. Gooch and A. C. McCorguodale. Before the commencement of the bitainess the chairman (Captain Withington rote I and said Before the proceedingo of to-day's Petty Sessions eminnence I wish,as chairman, and having been personallv acquainted with the late Mr. Joseph Evans.to expreas tire sympathy of the Bench with his family in their bereavement. 1 can remember perfectly well Mr. Evans sitting here just 21 years ago for the first time with myself and other magistrates. and although he has been prevented by his age and infirmity from attending here fort good many yoars, I should not like the pro- ceedings to commence to-day without an expression of the feeling of the Bench no his deceave.—Mr. Thomas Swift, barrister Liviniool, said Mr. eliairtnan. on , behalf of myself and the other advocates usually practising in this court 1 take this opportunity of express- ing our concurrence with the remarks winch have fallen from the chair, and our sympathy with the family la the late Mr. EMI, Thl• busituss woo then ',mood.' with.
DYSON'S DIORAMA AND GIPSY CHOIR
AT THE PUBLIC HALL.

Mr. Dyson and his excellent choir have again had a most gratifying reception at Warrington. At this time of the year, with line and open nights, most people have a strong partiality for outdoor amuse- ments and recreation, yet, in spite of this, the Public Hall has been very largely attended on each night during the week. This fact, of itself, speaks eloquently of the merits of the entertainment Mr.: Dyson provides. On Monday night,the Public Hall , was filled in every part. The subject for pictorial: representation was "Canada," and, the first view I being one of a scene in London, the spectator was carried in a series of admirable exhibi- tions from this country to the great colony across the Atlantic. Ile was shown faithful represen- tations of one of the "greyhounds of the Atlantic" I —the City of Rome -the public buildings of the I principal Canadian cities, the falls of Niagara, and , other objects and scenes of interest. In connection with each view, interesting explanations are given by Mr. Dyson. In the course of the evening a! pleasing musical entertainment is given by the 1 Gipsy Choir, and in this connection it may be men- tioned that each evening seven musical items are ! rendered before the room is darkened for the I diorama, five between the wpresentations, and sisc afterwards. On Monday evening the chair was taken by the Rev. W. Graham,and towards the close a vote of thanks was accorded him on the motion of : Mr. Dyson. The Chairman, in reply, said he was ' much obliged for having had the privilege to be 1 present. He had been very pleased indeed with the entertainment, which had been both elevating and , 1 instrnctive. Entertainments of the kind were 1 necessary to supplant those that were not so moral in their character, awl he wished Mr. Dyson success in his endeavours to provide relined entertainments such as they had had that evening. (Applause.) On Tuesday evening the subject for representation was India, and 1 the Chairman was the Rev. J. Yonge. In opening ! the proceedings, he said lie was at a loss to under- : . stand why it was considered the services of a Chair-1 man were requisite for a gathering like the present, ' but he supposed it WIIS for the purpose of , enabling one who occupied such a position to expre. his sympathy with a movement which had for its object not only amusement but instruction. (Hear, bear.) Ile had been given to understand that the entertainment which Mr. Dyson provided combined both those elements, and lie had no doubt that was one reason why that , gentleman had succeed in drawing such a large audience on a summer evening. Ile wile , quite sure they would all be fully repaid for coming !to listen to tile entertainment. It would not be be- -1 coming of him to attempt to make a speech. India was, of course, to all of them as English people very ; attractive and interesting, teeing that it belonged ' to the British empire ; and they would witness scenes that night -he was almost going to say in , their own country -at any rate in their own king- . dam which would be interesting, and bear things I about their fellow-subjects in that great empire across the sea. (Applauso.)- -On Wednesday even- ; ing "Wales " Was illustrated (the chair being tilled by Mr. J. Evans) ; on Thursday evening "London I to Land's End 't and last evening " Paris." To-night )fillillrdoy is the " People's night," and 1" Round the World is the subject for representa- I Hon. To-morrow afternoon and evening there will be sacred song services.

div.p: THE TRADE DISPUTES AT WARRINGTON.

TIIE EUDDLERS. During the present week the strike of underhand puddlers at the Hewsey and Dallain forges has approached no nearer u settlement, but the strike injection has spread to other works in the town. The underhand men employed by Messrs. Monks Hall & Co., and the White Cross Company, followed the example of the Bewsey and Dallam men, and there being no compliance with their demand for the bounty shilling, a strike at each place , followed. It is stated that some of the men have some I TEETII• out against their will, anti it is expected that they will return to work on the old terms before long. Many of !rum the strikers are said to be wishful to get hack to the forges without the bounty shilling, but are afraid to return, fearing their actmn might create an unplea.sant TEETH. feeling among the majority of the trivia. On Themday night the firm of hlerors. Monks, Hall and Co., conditionally conmded the bounty shilling to their men er EETII. on the understanding that if trade is slack at the end of three months time their wages will he reduced to the rate existing before the strike. Things 'TEETH. retnain mottled at the other places, and our reporter I_ was yesterday informed that the other masters will remain lion in their intention not to grant the bounty 'TEETH. shilling. As the largest firm in Lancashire, the action -IL taken bv the masters at Dallam and liewsey has bom imperative. For a few mars past they have been TEETH. actually losing money on the puddling, and, contrary to what is asserted by the men, our n.presentative was TEETH. informed that for the year eliding the 30th inst. the .1111.fied enonums increase in trade will nit amount to 2 per cent. over that of the preceding 12 months. rakmegir. Though no underhand peddlers are employed, the forw hands employ-id by the firm are still at work, and have shown no signs of a dmire to do the contrary. 'TEETH. THE COOPERS , AN IMPORTANT DEVELOPMENT. Inquiries made yesterday have elicited the fact that the tampers at the brewery of Mess.. Walker and Sons TEETH. are still firm in their intention to hold out for an altera- thin in the scale of wages, but there .4.11,, to he an rETII equally firm resolve on the part of the masters not to , • concede their demands. The strike of the hands would I appear tit have tern the occasion for unlooked.for action I'PEETII. by the firtn. During the past two or three days they , have completed arrangements for the repair of their barrels at Burton. Staffordshire, at the small Kiev "f 'TEETH. 514. each, while, it is stated, the Warrington coopers were paid 10.1, per barrel. Our representative was informed that Messrs. .Walker and Sons will, in future, 'TEETH. have the whole of their empering done at that town, IL anti that it is their intent ion to erect a cooperage t heron, only for the repair if the casks, but also he. making now barrels. The masters are convincol that this will result in a large saving to the firm. It is further statnl to be! the intention of the firm not to again take in their em- ploy many of the men who have mine out on strike. At present there are two regular coopers on day-work and one in pi-rework employed ..t Walker's cooperage in Dallatn-lane. The wages of tine man, fur the repair of ranks, on piecework and on the system under whieli the old hands refuse to work, were for the present week £2 13t. 9d. In reply to a statement issuol on behalf of the men, Mr. Cox says he asked all the old coopers to begin new work whom he thought were capable of doing new work, and, in regard to stopping men whim lie had to asked. he added that he only stopped one mats after the individual had been away, without notice, for three weeks. It io reported that one of the coopers at present work- ing for Messrs. Walker has this week been molested on it,, way home. Bags of soft, he., are bed t have been thrown at him, anti that one man personally threatened him with his ti.d
